mainTopic: משה's bold prayers for ישראל after חטא העגל, and praising God before asking
overview: The amud opens with verses showing that God plays a role in ישראל's conduct, which gives them a way to stand in judgment. רבי אלעזר then says משה spoke boldly toward God. דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי read וְדִי זָהָב as משה blaming the abundant gold for the עגל, and a series of parables and verses shows that plenty can lead to sin. The גמרא then follows משה's prayers after חטא העגל: God tells him to 'descend', משה realizes the matter depends on him, refuses to become a new nation, and pleads for ישראל. Many readings of the word וַיְחַל describe how far משה went in prayer. The גמרא explains further words of his plea, including God's eternal oath and the nations' claim that God was too weak, and shows that God agreed with him: 'סלחתי כדבריך'. רבי שמלאי learns from משה that one should praise God before making requests. The amud ends with a סימן listing teachings about the greatness of תפלה that begin on the next amud.

steps.title: Three verses give ישראל a way to stand
steps.stepSummary: After repeating a verse from the preceding discussion, רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא introduces three verses that matter when יִשְׂרָאֵל faces judgment.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: ‘And those with whom I have dealt badly.’ רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא said: Were it not for these three verses, the legs of ‘the enemies of יִשְׂרָאֵל’ would have given way.
steps.whatsHappening: The opening quote continues an earlier discussion. The new statement sets up a list of three verses that will explain why יִשְׂרָאֵל can still stand in judgment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase ‘the enemies of יִשְׂרָאֵל’ is a respectful way of referring to יִשְׂרָאֵל itself. The statement announces the importance of the verses; it has not listed them yet.

keyTerms.meaning: their legs would have given way
literally, ‘the enemies of Israel’; here a respectful substitute for Israel

phrases.english: As it is written: ‘And those with whom I have dealt badly.’
Rabbi Ḥama, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
Were it not for these three verses,
the legs of the enemies of Israel would have given way.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: אִלְמָלֵא שָׁלֹשׁ מִקְרָאוֹת הַלָּלוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opening citation carries over from discussion on the previous amud; the attributed statement begins a new list of supporting verses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three verses give יִשְׂרָאֵל grounds to stand when facing judgment.

steps.title: The three verses explain why ישראל can answer
steps.stepSummary: The promised verses speak of God’s role in wrongdoing, of יִשְׂרָאֵל as clay in God’s hand, and of God replacing a hard heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: One verse says, ‘And those with whom I have dealt badly.’ Another says, ‘Like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, house of יִשְׂרָאֵל.’ A third says, ‘I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.’
steps.whatsHappening: The statement now supplies its three verses. Each one adds a different way to see God’s involvement in what happens to יִשְׂרָאֵל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse attributes an adverse action to God; the second compares יִשְׂרָאֵל to clay shaped by a potter. The third promises that God will change people’s hearts. These verses give context for human wrongdoing without saying that people have no responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: and those with whom I have dealt badly
like clay in the potter’s hand

phrases.english: One is where it is written: ‘And those with whom I have dealt badly,’
and another is where it is written: ‘Behold, like clay in the potter’s hand,
so are you in My hand, house of Israel,’
and another is where it is written: ‘I will remove the heart of stone
from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.’

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This supplies the three verses promised in the preceding statement.
steps.raayaObject: God’s involvement is relevant when considering יִשְׂרָאֵל’s wrongdoing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The three quoted verses: וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי; the clay in the potter’s hand; and the promised replacement of a heart of stone.

steps.title: A further verse speaks of God causing obedience
steps.stepSummary: רַב פָּפָּא adds a verse that explicitly connects God’s placing His spirit within people to their walking in His laws.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַב פָּפָּא said: A source is here: ‘I will place My spirit within you, and I will bring it about that you walk in My statutes.’
steps.whatsHappening: רַב פָּפָּא adds another supporting verse. This one directly says that God will bring about people’s walking in His laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier verses described God’s influence through images and a promised change of heart. This verse states the connection to conduct more directly: God will place His spirit within them and cause them to follow His statutes.

keyTerms.meaning: from here; this is the source
I will place My spirit within you
you will walk in My statutes

steps.whatToRemember: The list gives three verses, then רַב פָּפָּא adds a fourth. His verse states most directly that God influences whether people follow His laws.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: A source is from here:
‘And I will place My spirit within you,
and I will bring it about that you walk in My statutes.’

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a more explicit supporting verse after the original list of three.
steps.raayaObject: God’s role in shaping whether people follow His laws.
steps.raayaSupportSource: וְאֶת רוּחִי אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם וְעָשִׂיתִי אֵת אֲשֶׁר בְּחֻקַּי תֵּלֵכוּ

steps.title: משה spoke boldly toward God
steps.stepSummary: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר says מֹשֶׁה spoke sharply toward God and reads “אֶל ה׳” as “עַל ה׳” to bring out that meaning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר said that מֹשֶׁה spoke boldly toward God. The verse says that מֹשֶׁה prayed “to God,” but he reads it as “upon God.”
steps.whatsHappening: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר makes a new statement about how מֹשֶׁה spoke to God. He immediately gives an interpretive reading of a verse to support it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse normally says that מֹשֶׁה prayed “to” God. Reading “upon” instead makes his words sound more forceful.

keyTerms.meaning: do not read it as; an instruction to interpret the wording differently

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: מֹשֶׁה הֵטִיחַ דְּבָרִים
phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said: Moses spoke sharply
toward God on high, as it is stated:
“And Moses prayed to the Lord.”
Do not read “to the Lord,”
but rather “upon the Lord.”

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: מֹשֶׁה הֵטִיחַ דְּבָרִים כְּלַפֵּי מַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The discussion moves from verses about God’s help to a new statement about מֹשֶׁה’s words toward God.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר says מֹשֶׁה spoke boldly toward God and supports this with the reading “עַל ה׳.”

steps.title: A basis for the changed reading
steps.stepSummary: The reading “עַל ה׳” is explained through a practice of reading א and ע in place of one another.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב read alefs as ayins and ayins as alefs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the previous step can move from “אֶל” to “עַל.” It points to a way these two letters were read interchangeably.
steps.deeperAnalysis: “אֶל” begins with א, while “עַל” begins with ע. This letter exchange supplies the basis for the interpretive reading; it does not say that the written verse has changed.

keyTerms.meaning: the school of רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן דְּבֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
phrases.english: For the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
read alefs as ayins,
and ayins as alefs.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁכֵּן דְּבֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב קוֹרִין לָאַלְפִין עַיְינִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It supplies the letter-reading basis for the interpretation in step 4.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The reading practice attributed to דְּבֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב.

steps.title: A different verse needs explaining
steps.stepSummary: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי turn to “וְדִי זָהָב” and ask what those words mean here.
steps.simpleTranslation: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי say the support comes from here: “וְדִי זָהָב.” What does “וְדִי זָהָב” mean?
steps.whatsHappening: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי introduce a different verse to support the claim about מֹשֶׁה. The question sets up the next move: explaining how this short phrase can be relevant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply quoting “וְדִי זָהָב” does not yet show what מֹשֶׁה said toward God. The question asks for the reading that will make it evidence.

keyTerms.meaning: the verse’s phrase that is about to be explained

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say: From here:
“And Di Zahav.”
What does “And Di Zahav” mean?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי אָמְרִי, מֵהָכָא: ״וְדִי זָהָב״. מַאי ״וְדִי זָהָב״?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Instead of explaining the א-to-ע reading, it opens a different route to support the same claim.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How “וְדִי זָהָב” speaks to מֹשֶׁה’s bold words toward God.

steps.title: משה points to the wealth given to ישראל
steps.stepSummary: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי explain “וְדִי זָהָב” as מֹשֶׁה saying that the abundant silver and gold given to יִשְׂרָאֵל led them to make the עֵגֶל.
steps.simpleTranslation: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי say that משה spoke before God: Master of the Universe, the silver and gold You gave ישראל were so abundant that they said “enough”; that wealth caused them to make the עגל.
steps.whatsHappening: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי answer their question by presenting the phrase as words מֹשֶׁה said to God. He points to the wealth God gave יִשְׂרָאֵל as a cause of the עֵגֶל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The explanation connects “דִּי” with “enough” and “זָהָב” with gold. It supports the claim that מֹשֶׁה spoke boldly: when defending יִשְׂרָאֵל, he brought God’s generous gift into his account of what led to their wrongdoing.

keyTerms.meaning: that You lavished or gave abundantly

steps.whatToRemember: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי use “וְדִי זָהָב” as a second way to show how boldly מֹשֶׁה spoke on behalf of יִשְׂרָאֵל.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: This is what Moses said before the Holy One, blessed be He:
Master of the Universe,

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁבִיל כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב שֶׁהִשְׁפַּעְתָּ לָהֶם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל,
phrases.english: because of the silver and gold that You lavished upon them, upon Israel,
until they said “enough”—
it caused them to make the calf.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי: כָּךְ אָמַר מֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It explains the verse introduced in step 6 and shows why that verse supports the claim in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: “וְדִי זָהָב” is read as מֹשֶׁה telling God that the abundance of silver and gold given to יִשְׂרָאֵל caused them to make the עֵגֶל.

steps.title: A lion roars over meat, not straw
steps.stepSummary: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי use a lion to illustrate the effect of having plenty.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רַבִּי יַנַּאי say: A lion does not roar from a basket of straw, but from a basket of meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds an illustration to the explanation of וְדִי זָהָב. The lion has something valuable in the basket of meat, not in the basket of straw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous step connected יִשְׂרָאֵל’s abundant gold with the עֵגֶל. This saying makes the broader point that having plenty can help bring out troublesome behavior.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:
A lion does not roar
from a basket of straw,
but from a basket of meat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the connection between abundance and wrongdoing stated in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vivid saying presents abundance as something that can bring out troublesome behavior.

steps.title: The well-fed cow kicks its owner
steps.stepSummary: רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא gives a second illustration: a cow kicks the person who fed it well.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא compares it to a person with a lean, large-limbed cow. He fed it lupines, and it kicked him. He says that the lupines he fed it caused the kicking.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another illustration of the same idea. This time, the animal acts against the very person who gave it good food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The food changes the cow’s situation: after being fed, it kicks its owner. This sharpens the point of וְדִי זָהָב—the gift itself can become part of the explanation for the recipient’s bad action.

keyTerms.meaning: lupines, used here as good feed

phrases.english: Rabbi Oshaya said:
A comparison: a person had
a lean, large-limbed cow.
He fed it lupines, and it kicked him.
He said to it: What caused you
to kick me—
if not the lupines I fed you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second illustration and emphasizes wrongdoing directed toward the giver.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Good food can become part of the explanation for the cow’s kicking.

steps.title: The father places his son near temptation
steps.stepSummary: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן gives a human example in which a father provides every comfort and then places his son near temptation.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא says in the name of רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: A man bathed, anointed, fed, and gave drink to his son, hung a purse around his neck, and seated him at the entrance to prostitutes. What could the son do to avoid sin?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from animal illustrations to a human one. Its closing question stresses how difficult it is for the son to resist after receiving comfort, money, and access to temptation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each action adds to the situation: the son is cared for, given money, and brought to the place of temptation. The question highlights the giver’s role in creating those conditions; it does not say that the son did not sin.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

phrases.aramaic: מָשָׁל לְאָדָם אֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ בֵּן.
phrases.english: A comparison: a certain man had a son.
He bathed and anointed him,
fed him and gave him drink,
and hung a purse around his neck,
and seated him at the entrance to prostitutes.
What can that son do
so that he will not sin?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Recasts the giver-and-recipient illustration as a human situation with temptation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Providing comfort and opportunity can make wrongdoing much harder to resist.

steps.title: A popular saying gains support from a verse
steps.stepSummary: רַב שֵׁשֶׁת cites a saying about a full stomach and points to a verse describing satisfaction, pride, and forgetting God.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַב אַחָא, son of רַב הוּנָא, says in the name of רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: This is what people say: A full belly brings bad behavior. As it is stated: When they were fed and became satisfied, their hearts rose, and therefore they forgot Me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now states the shared idea as a popular saying and brings a verse in its support. The verse links being satisfied with pride and forgetting God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier examples showed how plenty might lead to wrongdoing. Here the quoted verse gives that sequence explicitly: satisfaction, a lifted heart, then forgetting God.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa, son of Rav Huna, said that Rav Sheshet said:
This is what people say:
A full belly brings bad behavior.
As it is stated:
“As they were fed, they became satisfied;
they were satisfied and their hearts rose;
therefore they forgot Me.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from illustrations to a saying supported by a verse.
steps.raayaObject: The link between satisfaction and turning away from God.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ״כְּמַרְעִיתָם וַיִּשְׂבָּעוּ שָׂבְעוּ וַיָּרׇם לִבָּם עַל כֵּן שְׁכֵחוּנִי״

steps.title: Another verse links pride with forgetting God
steps.stepSummary: רַב נַחְמָן supplies a different verse for the link between a lifted heart and forgetting God.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַב נַחְמָן says: From here: “Your heart will rise, and you will forget the Lord.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another verse supporting the same warning. This verse focuses on the link between pride and forgetting God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous verse began with being fed and satisfied. This one states the next part of the sequence directly: the heart rises, and the person forgets God.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said: From here:
“Your heart will rise,
and you will forget the Lord.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different verse for the connection just supported in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: A lifted heart leads to forgetting God.

steps.title: A third verse links eating with turning away
steps.stepSummary: רַבָּנַן bring a third verse, moving from eating and satisfaction to turning away.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן say: From here: “He ate, became satisfied and fat, and turned away.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more verse for the same overall idea. Its wording starts with eating and ends with turning away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the verse cited by רַב נַחְמָן, this one includes eating and satisfaction in the quoted words. It therefore states both the abundance and the troubling response in one short passage.
steps.whatToRemember: The illustrations and verses all develop the point behind וְדִי זָהָב: abundance can help explain how people came to turn away.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say, from here:
“He ate, became satisfied and fat,
and turned away.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third verse, this time naming both satisfaction and turning away.
steps.raayaObject: Eating to satisfaction can be followed by turning away.

steps.title: One more verse links plenty with rebellion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another verse for the link between becoming well-fed and turning away.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you wish, learn it from here: “ישורון grew fat and kicked.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more possible verse to the series of proofs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse puts the two events side by side: ישורון becomes fat and then kicks. That supports the link the previous verses were establishing.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: from here:
“Jeshurun grew fat and kicked.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fourth possible verse to the same line of proof.
steps.raayaObject: Abundance can be followed by rebellion.

steps.title: A verse acknowledges the danger of the wealth
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני, citing רבי יונתן, brings a verse in which God says that He gave the people silver and gold, which they used for בעל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in רבי יונתן’s name: How do we know that הקדוש ברוך הוא later acknowledged משה’s point? As it says: “I increased silver for them, and gold they made for בעל.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks for evidence that God acknowledged משה’s point about the wealth given to ישראל. It answers by quoting a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse names God as the giver of the riches and then describes their misuse. This supports משה’s claim about how the riches contributed to the sin; it does not excuse the sin.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yonatan said:
From where do we know that the Holy One later returned
and acknowledged Moses’ point? As it is said:
“And I increased silver for them,
and gold they made for Baal.”

steps.triggerLanguage: מִנַּיִן שֶׁחָזַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְהוֹדָה לוֹ לְמֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from verses linking plenty and sin to a verse presented as God's acknowledgment of that link.
steps.raayaObject: God acknowledged משה’s point about the riches given to ישראל.

steps.title: What does “go down” mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes God's command to משה and asks what “go down” means here.
steps.simpleTranslation: “The Lord spoke to משה: Go down.” What does “go down” mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a different verse and sets up the next explanation by asking about the words “לֶךְ רֵד.”
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question focuses on why God tells משה to descend. The next step will read those words as more than an instruction to move.

phrases.english: “The Lord spoke to Moses: Go down.”
What does “go down” mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new reading of God's conversation with משה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the command ״לֶךְ רֵד״.

steps.title: משה is told to descend from his position
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains that משה’s standing was given for the sake of ישראל, and describes how this message weakened him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: הקדוש ברוך הוא told משה, “Descend from your greatness. I gave you greatness only for ישראל’s sake. Now that ישראל has sinned, why do I need you?” Immediately משה lost strength and could not speak.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question about “לֶךְ רֵד” and describes משה’s first reaction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here, “descend” refers to משה’s position, which served ישראל. Hearing that they had sinned left him too shaken to speak for them.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: The Holy One said to Moses:
Moses, descend from your greatness!
Did I give you greatness
for any reason other than Israel?
And now Israel has sinned—
why do I need you?
Immediately, Moses’ strength weakened,
and he had no strength to speak.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers what ״לֶךְ רֵד״ means and shows its immediate effect on משה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: God tells משה to descend from the standing he received for ישראל's sake.

steps.title: A warning gives משה the courage to pray
steps.stepSummary: When משה hears “leave Me be,” he realizes his response matters, and he prays for mercy.
steps.simpleTranslation: But when God said, “Leave Me be and I will destroy them,” משה said, “This matter depends on me!” He immediately stood, strengthened himself in prayer, and asked for mercy.
steps.whatsHappening: The account now shows what changes משה’s reaction: he hears that he is being told to step aside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה understands “leave Me be” to mean that his involvement can make a difference. He moves from being unable to speak to actively praying for ישראל.

phrases.english: And once He said, “Leave Me be and I will destroy them,”

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מֹשֶׁה: דָּבָר זֶה תָּלוּי בִּי!
phrases.english: Moses said: This matter depends on me!
Immediately he stood and strengthened himself in prayer,
and asked for mercy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how משה moves from weakness to prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה takes the command to step aside as a sign that his prayer can help.

steps.title: A parable explains the change
steps.stepSummary: A king’s friend is initially afraid to intervene, but the king’s own words show him that he can save the son.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like a king who angrily gave his son a severe beating. The king’s friend sat there, afraid to speak. The king said, “If not for this friend sitting before me, I would have killed you.” The friend realized, “This depends on me,” and immediately stood and saved the son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a parable to make משה’s change from silence to action easier to understand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The friend does not first know whether he may help. When the king says the friend is already holding him back, the friend understands that he should intervene.

phrases.english: A parable: a king became angry with his son,
and was striking him with a severe beating.
And his friend was sitting before him,
afraid to say anything to him.
The king said: If not for this friend of mine
who sits before me, I would have killed you.
He said: This matter depends on me.
Immediately he stood and saved him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates why hearing “leave Me be” led משה to pray.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A statement that someone is holding back a punishment tells that person that intervening can help.

steps.title: משה refuses to let the request for mercy go
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו reads “leave Me be” as a striking picture of משה holding on and insisting that God forgive ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: “Now leave Me be, so My anger may burn against them and I may consume them, and I will make you a great nation,” and so on. רבי אבהו said: If the verse were not written, we could not say this. It teaches that משה held on to הקדוש ברוך הוא like someone grasping a friend’s garment, saying, “Master of the Universe, I will not let You go until You forgive and pardon them.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes “leave Me be” again, and רבי אבהו gives it a stronger, vivid reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words suggest to רבי אבהו that משה would not stop pleading. The image of grasping a garment expresses his insistence; it is a way of explaining the verse, not a physical description of God.

phrases.english: “And now leave Me be,
so My anger may burn against them and I may consume them,
and I will make you a great nation,” and so on.
Rabbi Abbahu said:
If the verse were not written,
it would be impossible to say this.

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁתְּפָסוֹ מֹשֶׁה לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: It teaches that Moses grasped the Holy One,

phrases.aramaic: כְּאָדָם שֶׁהוּא תּוֹפֵס אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ בְּבִגְדוֹ,
phrases.english: like a person who grasps a friend by his garment,
and said before Him: Master of the Universe,
I will not let You go until You forgive
and pardon them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: אִלְמָלֵא מִקְרָא כָּתוּב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the parable to the verse and develops its picture of משה’s prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אבהו reads ״הַנִּיחָה לִּי״ as showing משה’s determined plea for forgiveness.

steps.title: A three-legged chair versus a one-legged chair
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains משה's answer to God's offer: if the merit of all three אבות could not stand up to God's anger, משה's merit alone certainly could not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'And I will make of you a great nation.' רבי אלעזר said: משה said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the world, a chair with three legs cannot stand before You when You are angry. A chair with one leg certainly cannot!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next part of God's words to משה, the offer to start a new nation from him. רבי אלעזר explains why משה turned the offer down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'three legs' stand for אברהם, יצחק, and יעקב. Their combined merit was not enough to protect ישראל from God's anger, so a nation built on משה's merit alone (one leg) would be even less stable. This is a simple קל וחומר: from the stronger case to the weaker one.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And I will make of you a great nation': God's offer to משה
A three-legged chair, a picture of the merit of the three אבות
At the time of Your anger
All the more so: the ending of a קל וחומר

steps.confusionAlert: The 'chair' here is not a real chair. It is a picture: each leg stands for the merit of one forefather holding up the nation.

phrases.english: "And I will make of you a great nation, etc."
phrases.notes: Exodus 32:10, the end of the same verse quoted earlier.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: Moses said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the Universe,
if a chair with three legs

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לַעֲמוֹד לְפָנֶיךָ בִּשְׁעַת כַּעְסֶךְ.
phrases.english: cannot stand before You at the time of Your anger,
a chair with one leg,
all the more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from 'leave Me be' to the next phrase of the same verse and gives משה's reply to God's offer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה refused to become a new nation because his merit alone could not withstand God's anger where the three אבות' merit had not.

steps.title: משה's shame before the אבות
steps.stepSummary: משה gives a second reason: the אבות would accuse him of taking greatness for himself instead of praying for ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And more than that, I would be ashamed in front of my forefathers. They would say: Look at the leader God put over them! He asked for greatness for himself, and he did not ask for mercy for them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר continues משה's words with a second reason for refusing God's offer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first reason was practical: one person's merit is too weak. This second reason is moral: a true leader cannot accept honor that comes from his people's destruction. So משה's job is to pray for them, not to replace them.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but also: adds a further point

steps.whatToRemember: משה refuses God's offer for two reasons: his merit alone is too weak (the one-legged chair), and a leader must ask mercy for his people, not greatness for himself.

phrases.english: Moreover,
I would feel shame before my forefathers;
now they will say:
See the leader that He placed over them!
He sought greatness for himself
and did not ask for mercy for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ בִּי בּוֹשֶׁת פָּנִים מֵאֲבוֹתַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, moral reason to the first, practical reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Accepting greatness at ישראל's expense would shame משה before the אבות; a leader must pray for his people.

steps.title: משה prayed until he became ill
steps.stepSummary: On the word וַיְחַל, רבי אלעזר teaches that משה prayed so intensely that it made him sick.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'And משה beseeched (וַיְחַל) before God.' רבי אלעזר said: This teaches that משה stood praying before הקדוש ברוך הוא until it made him ill.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next verse, which uses the unusual word וַיְחַל. רבי אלעזר gives the first of several explanations of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר connects וַיְחַל to the root חלה, 'sickness.' So the word itself shows how hard משה prayed: he pushed himself until he was physically worn out. This fits our sugya about תפילה, which describes how much effort real prayer can take.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And he beseeched': the unusual word being explained
It teaches: introduces a lesson drawn from a verse
It made him ill (from the root חלה)

steps.confusionAlert: The steps that follow give several more readings of the same word וַיְחַל, from רבא, שמואל, רבא in the name of רב יצחק, the רבנן, and a ברייתא of רבי אליעזר הגדול. These are different explanations of one word, not separate events.

phrases.english: "And Moses beseeched before the Lord"
Rabbi Elazar said:
This teaches that Moses stood in prayer
before the Holy One, Blessed be He,
until it made him ill.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next verse and begins a set of explanations of the word וַיְחַל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: וַיְחַל means משה prayed until he became ill.

steps.title: משה annulled God's vow
steps.stepSummary: רבא reads וַיְחַל as 'annulling a vow.' He links it to the vow verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ' and to the rule that others can annul a person's vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: משה prayed until he annulled God's vow. Here it is written 'וַיְחַל,' and there, about vows, it is written 'he shall not break (לֹא יַחֵל) his word.' And the Master said: he himself cannot annul his vow, but others can annul it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second explanation of וַיְחַל. He brings a word-link to the laws of vows to support it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the laws of נדרים, 'לֹא יַחֵל' means a person may not break his own word, yet a חכם or court can release the vow for him. Using the same word here suggests that משה acted like the one releasing God's 'vow' to destroy ישראל. This is a bold picture of how powerful משה's prayer was.

keyTerms.meaning: He annulled His vow for Him
It is written here... and it is written there: a word-link between two verses
He shall not break his word (a verse about vows)
The Master said: quotes an earlier teaching

steps.confusionAlert: 'He cannot annul, but others can' explains why משה could do it: God, so to speak, does not undo His own vow, but someone else (משה) can release it.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
until he annulled His vow for Him.
It is written here: "vayḥal,"
and it is written there: "He shall not break his word";
and the Master said:
He himself cannot annul it,
but others can annul it for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר עַד שֶׁהֵפֵר לוֹ נִדְרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different meaning for the same word וַיְחַל, this time from the language of vows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: וַיְחַל means משה annulled God's vow, learned from 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ' and the rule that others can annul a vow.

steps.title: משה offered his life for ישראל
steps.stepSummary: שמואל reads וַיְחַל as giving up one's life, and proves it from משה's words 'erase me from Your book.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: This teaches that משה gave himself up to death for them, as it says: 'And if not, erase me, please, from Your book.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives the third explanation of וַיְחַל and backs it up with a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל connects וַיְחַל to חלל, a dead person. His proof is משה's own words later in the story, where he asks to be erased if ישראל are not forgiven. Like the earlier readings (sickness, annulling a vow), it shows how far משה went for his people, and the next steps add still more readings of the same word.

keyTerms.meaning: He gave himself over to death
As it is said: introduces a supporting verse
Erase me, please, from Your book

steps.whatToRemember: So far, וַיְחַל has three readings: רבי אלעזר says משה prayed until he became ill; רבא says he annulled God's vow; שמואל says he offered his life for ישראל. More readings follow in the next steps.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
This teaches that he gave himself over to death for them,
as it is stated:
"And if not, erase me, please, from Your book."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר מְלַמֵּד שֶׁמָּסַר עַצְמוֹ לְמִיתָה עֲלֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a third meaning for וַיְחַל. Further meanings follow in steps 26–28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: וַיְחַל means משה offered his life for ישראל, as shown by 'מְחֵנִי נָא מִסִּפְרְךָ.'

steps.title: משה brought down God's mercy on ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רבא, quoting רב יצחק, reads וַיְחַל as coming from 'הֻחֲלָה', meaning 'made to rest upon.' Through his prayer, משה caused מדת רחמים to rest on ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב יצחק: The word וַיְחַל teaches that משה caused מדת רחמים to come down upon them.
steps.whatsHappening: This is one more reading of the word וַיְחַל. Here it means משה made God's mercy 'rest upon' ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier readings took וַיְחַל to mean becoming sick, annulling a vow, or giving up one's life. This reading links the root ח-ל-ל to 'הֻחֲלָה', meaning to take effect or rest upon. The focus moves from what happened to משה to what his prayer achieved for ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: was made to rest upon / took effect
it teaches (introduces what a verse teaches us)

phrases.english: Rava said in the name of Rav Yitzchak:
It teaches that there was made to rest upon them
the attribute of mercy.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק: מְלַמֵּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another interpretation of וַיְחַל, after שמואל's reading in step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: וַיְחַל means that משה caused מדת רחמים to rest upon ישראל.

steps.title: Destroying ישראל would be unworthy of God
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן read וַיְחַל as related to חוּלִּין, meaning a profanation. משה argued that destroying ישראל would be beneath God's dignity.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן say: It teaches that משה said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the World! It would be a profanation for You to do such a thing.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן give yet another reading of וַיְחַל. They say it is the content of משה's argument: 'It is חולין for You.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous readings described how משה prayed or what his prayer did. This reading supplies the actual words of his argument. Destroying the nation God chose would be a desecration of His Name, so it is 'unbecoming' of Him.

keyTerms.meaning: it is a profanation for You / beneath You

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
It teaches that Moshe said
before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the World!
It is a profanation for You
to do such a thing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another parallel reading of וַיְחַל, alongside רבא's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: וַיְחַל means that משה told God that destroying ישראל would be חולין, a profanation unworthy of Him.

steps.title: משה prayed until he was struck by אחילו
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי אליעזר הגדול: משה stood in prayer until he was seized by אחילו.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And משה beseeched the face of ה׳.' It was taught: רבי אליעזר הגדול says: It teaches that משה stood in prayer before הקדוש ברוך הוא until he was seized by אחילו.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with one more reading of וַיְחַל. It uses an unfamiliar word, אחילו. This also sets up the next steps, which explain that word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a תנאי source, which carries more weight than the אמוראים before it. It links וַיְחַל to אחילו, a physical condition that came from intense prayer. The meaning of אחילו is unclear, so the גמרא will need to define it.

keyTerms.meaning: it was taught in a ברייתא
רבי אליעזר the Great (רבי אליעזר בן הורקנוס)
a rare word for an illness; it is defined in the next steps

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up רבי אליעזר הגדול, the תנא here, with רבי אלעזר, the אמורא in the next step who explains his word.

phrases.english: 'And Moshe beseeched the face of ה׳,'
It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says:
It teaches that Moshe stood in prayer
before the Holy One, Blessed be He
until he was seized by 'achilu.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A ברייתא reading of וַיְחַל. It is close to רבי אלעזר's 'sickness' reading in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה prayed so intensely that he was struck by אחילו.

steps.title: What is אחילו? A fire in the bones
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what אחילו means. רבי אלעזר answers: 'a fire of the bones.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is אחילו? רבי אלעזר said: A fire of the bones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to explain the unfamiliar word from the ברייתא. רבי אלעזר defines it in Hebrew as 'fire of the bones.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a question about the meaning of a word, not a challenge. The answer gives a Hebrew description of a burning illness. That phrase was still unclear to some learners, which leads to the next step.

phrases.english: What is 'achilu'?
Rabbi Elazar said:
A fire of the bones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the key word from the ברייתא in step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the rare word אחילו.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אלעזר: it is אש של עצמות, a fire of the bones.

steps.title: What is 'fire of the bones'? A burning fever
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'fire of the bones' means. אביי gives the common Aramaic name of the illness: אשתא דגרמי.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is 'fire of the bones'? אביי said: אשתא דגרמי, a bone-fever.
steps.whatsHappening: The definition still needed explaining, so the גמרא asks again. אביי gives the everyday Babylonian name for the illness, a high fever.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Hebrew phrase used in ארץ ישראל is translated into the spoken Aramaic of בבל. אשתא means fever and גרמי means bones. So אחילו is a burning fever that משה got from his intense prayer.
steps.whatToRemember: וַיְחַל can mean that משה prayed so hard he caught a burning fever (אחילו, which is אשתא דגרמי).

phrases.english: What is 'fire of the bones'?
Abaye said:
Ishta d'garmei (bone-fever).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the definition given in step 29.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What illness 'fire of the bones' refers to.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אביי: it is אשתא דגרמי, a burning fever.

steps.title: What does 'by Yourself' mean in משה's prayer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes משה's plea 'זכור לאברהם…אשר נשבעת להם בך' and asks what 'בך' (by Yourself) means.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Remember אברהם, יצחק, and ישראל Your servants, to whom You swore by Yourself.' What does 'by Yourself' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next verse of משה's prayer and asks about one word. This step sets up רבי אלעזר's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse could have just said 'You swore to them.' The extra word בך seems unnecessary, so the גמרא asks what it adds. The answer will show that it is the heart of משה's argument.

phrases.english: 'Remember Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yisrael Your servants,
to whom You swore by Yourself.'
What does 'by Yourself' mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the word וַיְחַל to the next part of משה's prayer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the extra word בך in the verse adds.

steps.title: An oath by God's eternal Name lasts forever
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains משה's argument. An oath sworn by heaven and earth would end when they end. God swore by His own eternal Name, so the oath lasts forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: משה said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the World, if You had sworn to them by heaven and earth, I would say: just as heaven and earth will pass away, so too Your oath will pass away. But now that You swore to them by Your great Name, just as Your great Name lives and endures forever and ever, so too Your oath endures forever and ever.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question about בך. משה argued that God's promise to the אבות cannot be cancelled, because it was sworn by God's eternal Name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument works by comparison. An oath lasts only as long as the thing it was sworn by. Heaven and earth are temporary, but God's Name is eternal. So destroying ישראל would break a promise that can never end.
steps.whatToRemember: בך means God swore by His own Name. Since His Name is eternal, His promise to the אבות, and so His bond with ישראל, can never be cancelled.
steps.whyThisMatters: This strengthens משה's case for ישראל. In step 21 he argued that even the three אבות' merit could not stand before God's anger, so his own merit alone certainly could not. Now he relies on God's oath to the אבות, which is permanent because it was sworn by God's eternal Name.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: Moshe said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the World,
had You sworn to them
by heaven and earth,
I would say:
just as heaven and earth will pass away —
so too Your oath will pass away.
But now that You swore to them
by Your great Name,
just as Your great Name lives and endures
forever and ever —
so too Your oath endures
forever and ever.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about בך asked in step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: בך means by God's own eternal Name, so the oath to the אבות can never become void.

steps.title: Why does the verse say 'of which I have spoken'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes משה's plea and points out that the words 'אשר אמרתי' (I have spoken) seem wrong, because משה is talking about God's promise.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'And You said to them: I will make your children as many as the stars of heaven, and all this land of which I have spoken.' Why does it say 'of which I have spoken'? It should have said 'of which You have spoken'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps reading משה's prayer and raises a wording problem. It is setting up the explanations that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה is speaking to God and recalling God's oath to the אבות. So the land is the land God spoke about, and the grammar should be 'You have spoken' (אמרת), not 'I have spoken' (אמרתי). The גמרא wants to know why the verb switches to the first person.

keyTerms.meaning: It should have said (a standard way of flagging a wording problem)

phrases.english: "And You said to them:
I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven,
phrases.notes: שמות 32:13, part of משה's plea after חטא העגל

phrases.english: and all this land of which I have spoken"
This phrase "of which I have spoken"
should have said "of which You have spoken"!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי אֲשֶׁר אָמַרְתִּי אֲשֶׁר אָמַרְתָּ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues reading the same plea of משה, moving on to the next part of the verse.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the verse uses the first person 'I have spoken' when משה is speaking about God's promise.

steps.title: The speaker changes in the middle of the verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the first part of the verse is משה speaking, and from 'all this land of which I have spoken' it is God speaking.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: Up to this point, these are the words of the student (משה). From here on, these are the words of the Master (God).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers by splitting the verse between two speakers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If God is the one saying 'all this land of which I have spoken,' then 'I' is correct, because God is speaking about His own promise. So the grammar problem goes away: the verse quotes משה first and then God.

keyTerms.meaning: The words of the student (here, משה)
The words of the Master (here, God)

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
Up to here are the words of the student;
from here onward are the words of the Master.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד כָּאן דִּבְרֵי תַלְמִיד מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ דִּבְרֵי הָרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse has two speakers. משה speaks first, and God says 'all this land of which I have spoken,' so 'I' fits.

steps.title: משה spoke the whole verse about his own words
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני says משה said the whole verse. 'I have spoken' means: I already told Israel Your promise in Your name, so what do I tell them now?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said: Both parts are the words of the student. Rather, this is what משה said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the Universe, the things You told me, 'Go tell ישראל in My name,' I went and told them in Your name. Now what do I tell them?
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives a different answer. He keeps משה as the only speaker and explains 'I have spoken' as משה's own words to the people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'the land of which I have spoken' means the land משה himself promised the people when he passed along God's message. משה's point is that if God destroys them, משה's own words, said in God's name, will turn out false. That is another argument for God to forgive.

keyTerms.meaning: In My name / in Your name

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two answers. רבי אלעזר says God says the second half. רבי שמואל בר נחמני says משה says it all, and the 'I' is משה talking about what he told the people.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said:
These and those are the words of the student;
rather, this is what Moses said
before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the Universe,
the things that You told me,
"Go say them to Israel" in My name,
I went and told them in Your name.
Now what do I say to them?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי תַלְמִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different answer to the same question, disagreeing with רבי אלעזר about who is speaking.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: משה is the only speaker. 'I have spoken' refers to משה's own words to Israel, which would become false if they were destroyed.

steps.title: Why the odd word 'יכולת'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the verse uses the feminine noun 'יכולת' instead of the plain verb 'יכול'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'Because the Lord was without ability (יכולת).' It should have said 'the Lord was not able (יכול).'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to another prayer of משה, the one after the מרגלים, and flags an unusual word. This sets up רבי אלעזר's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The simple way to say 'God was not able' is with the masculine verb יכול. The verse instead uses יכולת, a feminine-sounding form. The גמרא assumes the unusual form is there for a reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of the lack of / without

phrases.english: "Because the Lord lacked the ability":
phrases.notes: במדבר 14:16, what the nations would say

phrases.english: It should have said "the Lord was [not] able."

steps.triggerLanguage: מִבִּלְתִּי יְכֹלֶת ה׳ יָכוֹל ה׳ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new verse and a different prayer of משה, using the same kind of close-reading question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the verse uses the feminine form יכולת instead of יכול.

steps.title: The nations will say God's strength weakened
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains that the feminine word hints at משה's argument: the nations will say God became weak like a female and cannot save.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: משה said before הקדוש ברוך הוא: Master of the Universe, now אומות העולם will say His strength has weakened like a female, and He cannot rescue.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the wording question. The feminine form reflects the insult the nations would use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The odd word is not a mistake. It hints at what the nations would claim: God's power has become 'weak like a female.' משה uses this as an argument that destroying Israel would cause a חילול השם.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: Moses said before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the Universe,
now the nations of the world will say
His strength has weakened like a female,
and He is unable to rescue.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר מֹשֶׁה לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The feminine form hints at the nations' claim that God's power grew weak like a female.

steps.title: God answers: they already saw the miracles at the sea
steps.stepSummary: הקדוש ברוך הוא pushes back on משה's argument: the nations already saw His great miracles at the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקדוש ברוך הוא said to משה: Didn't they already see the miracles and mighty acts that I did for them at the sea?
steps.whatsHappening: Inside רבי אלעזר's story, God challenges משה's claim. This sets up משה's reply in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה's argument depends on the nations thinking God is weak. God answers that קריעת ים סוף already proved His power, so nobody could seriously claim He cannot save.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses:
But did they not already see
the miracles and mighty acts that I performed for them
at the sea?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges משה's argument from step 37 within the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: משה's claim that the nations will say God cannot save.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The nations already saw God's power at the sea, so a claim that He is weak would not be believed.

steps.title: One king is not thirty-one kings
steps.stepSummary: משה answers that the nations could still say God beat one king, פרעה, but cannot beat the thirty-one kings of כנען.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said before Him: Master of the Universe, they can still say: He could stand up to one king, but He cannot stand up to thirty-one kings.
steps.whatsHappening: משה answers God's challenge and keeps his argument alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The miracle at the sea was against a single king, פרעה. Conquering ארץ ישראל means fighting thirty-one kings, so the nations could claim God's power has limits. That is why משה's fear of a חילול השם still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Thirty-one kings (the kings of כנען that יהושע defeated)

steps.whatToRemember: משה's prayers use God's honor as the argument. If Israel is destroyed, the nations will say God was too weak to bring them into the land. Even the miracle at the sea does not answer this, because one king is not thirty-one.

phrases.english: He said before Him:
Master of the Universe,
they can still say:
Against one king He was able to stand;

phrases.aramaic: לִשְׁלשִׁים וְאֶחָד מְלָכִים אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לַעֲמוֹד.
phrases.english: against thirty-one kings He is unable to stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers God's challenge from step 38.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the cases: one king versus many kings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The miracles at the sea already proved God's power, so the nations could not call Him weak.
steps.terutzMaskana: Beating one king does not prove He can beat thirty-one, so the nations could still question His power.

steps.title: God agreed with משה's argument
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן proves from the verse 'סלחתי כדבריך' that הקדוש ברוך הוא accepted משה's argument.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: How do we know that הקדוש ברוך הוא changed His mind and agreed with משה? Because the verse says: 'And ה׳ said: I have forgiven, according to your words.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן closes the debate between משה and God from the previous steps. He shows from a verse that God ended up agreeing with משה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 38-39, God pushed back and משה answered about the thirty-one kings. The word 'כדבריך', 'according to your words', shows that God forgave because of משה's argument itself. So משה's reasoning was accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: Agreed with him, conceded to him

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
From where do we know that the Holy One, Blessed be He, went back
and conceded to Moses?
As it is said: “And the Lord said:
I have forgiven according to your words.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מִנַּיִן שֶׁחָזַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְהוֹדָה לוֹ לְמֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of משה's answer in step 39: God accepted it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word 'כדבריך' shows that God forgave Israel because He accepted משה's argument.

steps.title: The nations will one day say it
steps.stepSummary: דבי רבי ישמעאל read 'כדבריך' as: what you said will really happen, because the nations will say it in the future.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: 'According to your words' means that the nations of the world will indeed say this in the future.
steps.whatsHappening: A second reading of the same word 'כדבריך' is added. It means משה's prediction was correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן read 'כדבריך' as God agreeing with משה. דבי רבי ישמעאל add a sharper point. משה's warning was not only convincing. It was true, because the nations really would have said that God could not save Israel.

keyTerms.meaning: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught
They are destined to, in the future they will

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
“According to your words”:
phrases.notes: The word from the verse being explained.

phrases.english: the nations of the world will indeed say this in the future.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further reading of the word 'כדבריך' from step 40.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'כדבריך' means משה's prediction about what the nations would say was accurate.

steps.title: Fortunate is the student whose teacher agrees with him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws a lesson: a student is fortunate when his teacher accepts his words.
steps.simpleTranslation: Fortunate is the student whose teacher agrees with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up the story with a short lesson. God, the 'teacher', agreed with משה, the 'student'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a new derivation. It is a closing remark on what we just saw. Being agreed with by one's teacher is a great honor, and משה received it from God Himself.
steps.whatToRemember: משה argued for Israel, and God agreed with his words ('סלחתי כדבריך'). The גמרא calls a student whose teacher agrees with him fortunate.

phrases.english: Happy is the student whose teacher concedes to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a moral lesson from God agreeing with משה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is a great honor for a student when his teacher agrees with him, as God agreed with משה.

steps.title: You gave Me life with your words
steps.stepSummary: רבא in the name of רב יצחק explains 'ואולם חי אני' as God telling משה: 'You have given Me life with your words.'
steps.simpleTranslation: On the verse 'But as I live,' רבא said in the name of רב יצחק: This teaches that הקדוש ברוך הוא said to משה: 'משה, you have given Me life with your words.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next verse and gives a דרשה on the words 'חי אני'. God was pleased by משה's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of reading 'חי אני' only as an oath, רב יצחק reads it as 'you made Me live'. God was glad that משה's arguments gave Him a reason to forgive Israel. This continues the theme of God's warm approval of משה.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not take 'you gave Me life' literally. It is a figure of speech meaning God was pleased and delighted by משה's words.

phrases.english: “Nevertheless, as I live”:
Rava said that Rav Yitzchak said:

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: This teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses:
Moses, you have given Me life with your words.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְאוּלָם חַי אָנִי״, אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the next verse in the same passage, continuing the theme of God's approval of משה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'חי אני' teaches that God told משה, 'You have given Me life with your words.'

steps.title: First praise God, then pray
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמלאי teaches that a person should always set out praise of God first, and only then pray for his needs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמלאי taught: A person should always first arrange the praise of הקדוש ברוך הוא, and afterward pray.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins, still connected to משה's prayers. רבי שמלאי gives a general rule about the order of תפילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the גמרא told a story about משה. Now it draws a practical rule from משה's way of praying: praise comes before requests. This is why the שמונה עשרה begins with blessings of praise before the requests.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the structure of שמונה עשרה: the first blessings are praise, then come the requests.

phrases.english: Rabbi Simlai taught:
A person should always set forth
the praise of the Holy One, Blessed be He,
and afterward pray.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרַשׁ רַבִּי שִׂמְלַאי: לְעוֹלָם יְסַדֵּר אָדָם שִׁבְחוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the story of משה to a practical rule for תפילה learned from משה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should always praise God first and only then make personal requests.

steps.title: What is the source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבי שמלאי's rule comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of רבי שמלאי's rule. This sets up the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on the rule. It is a standard request for the source behind it. The answer will come from a verse.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know it?

phrases.english: From where do we derive this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule stated in step 44.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for praising God before praying for one's needs.

steps.title: משה praised God before asking to enter the land
steps.stepSummary: The source is משה's prayer in ואתחנן. He first praised God's greatness, and only afterward asked to cross into ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn it from משה, as it is written: 'And I pleaded with ה׳ at that time.' And it is written: 'ה׳ אלקים, You have begun to show Your servant Your greatness and Your strong hand, for what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do deeds like Yours and Your mighty acts?' And after that it is written: 'Please let me cross over and see the good land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing the order of משה's prayer. Praise comes first, and the request comes after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is from the order of the verses. משה said he was pleading, but his first words were praise of God's greatness. Only in the next verse did he make his personal request, 'Let me cross over'. This order is the model for every person's תפילה.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמלאי's rule is to praise God first and then ask. The source is משה in ואתחנן, who praised God's greatness before asking to enter the land.

phrases.english: From Moses, as it is written:
“And I beseeched the Lord at that time.”
And it is written: “Lord God, You have begun
to show Your servant Your greatness
and Your strong hand,
for what god is there in the heavens or on earth
who can perform deeds like Yours and Your mighty acts?”
And it is written after it:
“Please, let me pass over and see
the good land, etc.”

steps.triggerLanguage: מִמֹּשֶׁה, דִּכְתִיב: ״וָאֶתְחַנַּן אֶל ה׳ בָּעֵת הַהִיא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 45 with a proof from the order of verses.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: משה's prayer in ואתחנן opens with praise (3:24) and only afterward makes the request (3:25), so praise must come before requests.
steps.raayaObject: רבי שמלאי's rule that praise comes before requests.

steps.title: A memory list for the coming teachings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a סימן of seven key words. Each word hints at one of the upcoming statements about תפלה and related topics.
steps.simpleTranslation: Memory aid: Deeds, charity, offering, priest, fast, shoe (lock), iron.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is not teaching anything new yet. It is setting up the next section by giving a short word list to help us remember the teachings that are about to come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא was once learned by heart, so a סימן worked like a table of contents. Each word stands for one upcoming statement, mostly from רבי אלעזר, about how great תפלה is. For example, מעשים hints at the coming teaching that תפלה is greater than good deeds, which is learned from משה, so it connects to the topic we just finished.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid. A list of key words that hint at the teachings coming next.
A sacrifice or offering brought in the בית המקדש.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not try to find a teaching inside this line by itself. The words make no full sentence. They are only labels for the statements that come next, so you will understand each word once you reach its teaching.
steps.whyThisMatters: Spotting a סימן tells you that a new group of related teachings is starting. It also gives you a preview of how many teachings are coming and in what order.

phrases.english: Memory aid: deeds, charity,
phrases.notes: סימן signals that a list of key words follows. מעשים hints at the coming teaching that תפלה is greater than good deeds.

phrases.english: offering, priest, fast,
phrases.notes: Each word points to an upcoming statement. These include teachings about sacrifices, about a כהן, and about fasting.

phrases.english: shoe (lock), iron.
phrases.notes: מנעל is related to the root meaning 'to lock'. It likely hints at the coming teaching that the gates of תפלה were locked after the חורבן. ברזל hints at the teaching about an iron wall that now separates us from Heaven.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Setup / mnemonic line, which has no exact category
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The section about praising God before asking for one's needs, learned from משה's תפלה, is over. The גמרא now opens a new set of teachings on the greatness of תפלה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no ruling here. It is a list of key words that maps out the next seven teachings.
